alt.ex: Health care professionals must support their facility's decisions and practices. If that is impossible, the text says it may be best to seek employment elsewhere.
w: Keep the job but quietly refuse to take part
Workers must support facility practices.
Persuade patients to avoid the procedure
This imposes the nurse's own values on patients.
Report the clinic to the licensing board
A legal procedure is not a violation to report.

items.q: Improper or illegal professional activity leading to substandard treatment is called
items.ex: Malpractice is the textbook's term for improper, illegal or negligent professional activity or treatment, which leads to substandard care. Watch out: Negligence is the near miss: it is part of the definition, but the term for improper or illegal professional activity is malpractice.
w: negligence.
Negligence is failure to meet the expected standard of care. Malpractice is the broader term for improper professional activity.
abuse.
Abuse is mistreatment of a person, not substandard professional practice.
defamation.
Defamation is a false statement that damages someone's reputation.

alt.q: A health care worker forgets to raise a patient's bed rails, and the patient falls. Failing to take a necessary action like this is best described as
alt.a: negligence
alt.ex: Negligence is failure to meet the standard of care expected of someone with that training, and it can come from an action done wrong or from not taking a needed action.
w: assault
Assault is a threat or attempt to harm.
defamation
Defamation is a false statement that damages a reputation.
invasion of privacy
Invasion of privacy is exposing private information.

alt.q: According to the textbook, what is the best defense against malpractice lawsuits?
alt.a: Communicating a sincere, caring attitude
alt.ex: The text says communicating a sincere, caring attitude toward patients is the best defense, because patient anger and poor relationships are leading causes of lawsuits.
w: Carrying a large malpractice insurance policy
Insurance pays claims but does not prevent lawsuits.
Limiting conversation with patients
Poor relationships are a leading cause of lawsuits.
Charting only the normal findings
Incomplete charting increases risk.

items.q: The abbreviations IU, q.d., q.o.d., and U must appear on an accredited institution's "Do Not Use" list established by which organization?
items.ex: The Joint Commission requires accredited organizations to have a Do Not Use list that includes U, IU, q.d. and q.o.d. Watch out: ISMP also has an error-prone abbreviation list, but the list accredited institutions must use comes from The Joint Commission.
w: Centers for Disease Control
The CDC works to control disease spread. It does not accredit facilities or set documentation lists.
The Institute for Safe Medication Practices
ISMP publishes a broader list it recommends, but the required list for accredited institutions comes from The Joint Commission.
The World Health Organization
WHO is an international health agency, not a U.S. accrediting body.

alt.q: A provider writes 'Give 10 U insulin q.d.' Which rewrite follows the Do Not Use list?
alt.a: Give 10 units insulin daily
alt.ex: U must be written as 'units' and q.d. as 'daily', because both are on the Do Not Use list.
w: Give 10 IU insulin every day
IU is also on the list.
Give 10 U insulin daily
U is still used.
Give 10 units insulin q.d.
q.d. is still used.

alt.q: Why should 'q.o.d.' never be used in documentation?
alt.a: It can be misread as q.d. or q.i.d.
alt.ex: If the 'o' is poorly written, q.o.d. can be mistaken for q.d. (daily) or q.i.d. (four times a day), so 'every other day' is written out.
w: It is the Latin form of 'every hour'
It means every other day.
It must be written in capital letters
QOD in capitals is also on the list.
It means 'by mouth' in some facilities
Not true. The problem is misreading.

items.q: What does gastrectomy mean?
items.a: Removal of all or part of the stomach
items.ex: Gastr/o means stomach and -ectomy means surgical removal, so gastrectomy is removal of all or part of the stomach. Watch out: -otomy, -ectomy and -stomy look alike: incision, removal and opening.
w: An incision into the stomach
An incision into the stomach is a gastrotomy (-otomy).
Inflammation of the stomach
Inflammation of the stomach is gastritis (-itis).
An opening into the stomach
An opening into the stomach is a gastrostomy (-stomy).

alt.q: A surgeon creates an opening from the colon to the outside of the abdominal wall. Which term describes this?
alt.a: Colostomy
alt.ex: -stomy means a surgically created opening, so colostomy is an opening into the colon.
w: Colectomy
-ectomy means removal.
Colotomy
-otomy means incision.
Colitis
-itis means inflammation.

alt.q: Which pair of terms shares a suffix meaning 'surgical removal'?
alt.a: Appendectomy and lumpectomy
alt.ex: Both end in -ectomy (surgical removal): removal of the appendix and removal of a lump.
w: Appendicitis and tonsillitis
-itis means inflammation.
Gastrotomy and tracheotomy
-otomy means incision.
Colostomy and gastrostomy
-stomy means an opening.

items.q: What does the combination "ch" sound like in medical terminology?
items.ex: Table 5–6 says 'ch' in medical terms sounds like k, as in chronic. Watch out: Everyday English 'ch' (as in chair) makes the other sounds tempting, but in medical terms ch sounds like k.
w: s
c (not ch) sounds like s when followed by e, i or y.
g
g sounds like j before e, i or y, and no rule gives ch the sound of g.
h
ch is not pronounced as an h in medical terms.

alt.q: Which word begins with an f sound when pronounced?
alt.a: Pharmacist
alt.ex: Table 5–6 says ph sounds like f, as in pharmacist.
w: Psychiatrist
ps sounds like s.
Pneumonia
pn sounds like n.
Cholesterol
ch sounds like k.

alt.q: How is the first g in 'gingivitis' pronounced?
alt.a: Like j, because it is followed by i
alt.ex: Table 5–6 says g followed by e, i or y sounds like j, as in genetic and gingivitis.
w: Like k, because it begins the word
Being the first letter does not change the sound.
Like g in 'go,' since it is a hard g
Before i, the g is soft.
Like s, because a vowel follows it
The s rule applies to c, not g.

items.q: All medical terms have at least one
items.ex: Every medical term has at least one word root, the part that gives the main meaning. Prefixes, suffixes and combining vowels are used only as needed. Watch out: Suffix is the near miss: the text says all terms have a suffix UNLESS the root is a complete word by itself, so a suffix is not universal.
w: prefix.
Many terms have no prefix (for example, gastritis).
suffix.
Most terms have a suffix, but not when the word root is a complete word by itself.
combining vowel.
A combining vowel is used only when needed. It is dropped before a suffix that begins with a vowel.

alt.q: In 'gastritis,' why is there no combining vowel between gastr and -itis?
alt.a: The suffix begins with a vowel
alt.ex: When a suffix begins with a vowel, it is attached directly to the word root, as in gastritis.
w: The word root is a complete word
gastr is not a complete word by itself.
The term has no word root at all
gastr is the word root.
Combining vowels are used only with prefixes
The combining vowel links a root to a suffix or another root.

alt.q: Which part of 'bradycardia' gives the term its main meaning?
alt.a: cardi, the word root
alt.ex: The word root gives the main meaning (heart). The prefix brady- (slow) modifies it.
w: brady-, the prefix
The prefix changes the meaning (slow) but is not the main meaning.
-ia, the suffix
The suffix means condition.
o, the combining vowel
Bradycardia has no combining vowel, and a vowel carries no meaning.

items.q: Which of the following is an instrument used to examine the ear?
items.ex: Ot/o means ear and -scope means an instrument used to view, so an otoscope is the instrument for examining the ear. Watch out: All four share ot/o (ear), so only the suffix tells you which is an instrument.
w: Otology
Otology is the study of the ear (-logy).
Otitis
Otitis is inflammation of the ear (-itis).
Otoplasty
Otoplasty is surgical repair of the ear (-plasty).

alt.q: Which term names the procedure, rather than the instrument, for viewing the sigmoid colon?
alt.a: Sigmoidoscopy
alt.ex: -scopy means examination with a scope (the procedure). -scope is the instrument itself.
w: Sigmoidoscope
-scope names the instrument.
Sigmoidectomy
-ectomy means removal.
Sigmoiditis
-itis means inflammation.

alt.q: A provider uses an instrument to look inside a patient's eye. Based on word parts, the instrument is most likely called an
alt.a: ophthalmoscope
alt.ex: Ophthalm/o means eye and -scope means an instrument used to view.
w: otoscope
ot/o means ear.
ophthalmology
-logy means the study of.
ophthalmoplasty
-plasty means surgical repair.

items.q: 1100 in military time is the same as
items.ex: Military times below 1200 are morning hours, so 1100 is 11:00 a.m. 11:00 p.m. would be 2300. Watch out: With no a.m. or p.m. shown, 1100 can look ambiguous, but every time below 1200 is morning.
w: 00:11 is not the format, and 0011 would be 12:11 a.m.
Military time does not use a.m. or p.m. at all.

alt.q: A medication was charted as given at 2115. In traditional time, this is
alt.ex: 2115 is after 1200, so subtract 1200: 2115 − 1200 = 915, which is 9:15 p.m.
w: This drops the 1 and reads 2115 as 2:15; 2:15 p.m. would be 1415.
This subtracts 1000 instead of 1200.
Times above 1200 are p.m.

alt.q: A dose is due 6 hours after a dose given at 2200. At what military time is the next dose due?
alt.ex: 2200 + 6 hours passes midnight (2400): 22 + 6 = 28, and 28 − 24 = 4, which is 0400.
w: Military time stops at 2400 and starts over.
This subtracts 6 hours instead of adding them.
This counts 6 hours from midnight instead of from 2200.

items.q: The provider has ordered medication based on weight for a patient weighing 150 lbs. The medication is to be administered 5mg/kg. What is the correct dosage for the patient?
items.ex: First convert pounds to kilograms: 150 ÷ 2.2 = 68.2 kg. Then 68.2 kg × 5 mg/kg ≈ 341 mg, so 340 mg is correct. Watch out: The order is per kilogram but the weight is in pounds, so you must convert first. Every distractor matches a different body weight.
w: 300 mg
300 mg would be the dose for 60 kg (132 lb).
400 mg
400 mg would be the dose for 80 kg (176 lb).
450 mg
450 mg would be the dose for 90 kg (198 lb).

alt.q: A child weighs 44 lb. The order is 10 mg/kg. How many mg should be given?
alt.a: 200 mg
alt.ex: 44 lb ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg, and 20 kg × 10 mg/kg = 200 mg.
w: 440 mg
This uses pounds without converting to kilograms.
220 mg
This divides by 2 instead of 2.2, giving 22 kg.
20 mg
This gives the weight in kg, not the dose.

alt.q: A patient weighs 66 kg. The order is 3 mg/kg per day, divided into 2 equal doses. How much is each dose?
alt.a: 99 mg
alt.ex: 66 kg × 3 mg/kg = 198 mg per day, and 198 ÷ 2 = 99 mg per dose.
w: 198 mg
This is the daily total, not one dose.
This wrongly changes kilograms to pounds before multiplying.
45 mg
This treats 66 as pounds and divides by 2.2.

items.q: When is estimating used on the job by the health care worker?
items.a: To judge if calculated results are reasonable
items.ex: Health care workers estimate an approximate answer so they can judge whether a calculated result is reasonable and catch errors. Watch out: 'Increasing the efficiency of long calculations' sounds useful, but an estimate is used to check the exact calculation, not as a shortcut.
w: To increase the efficiency of performing long calculations
Estimating checks the exact calculation. It does not replace it or speed it up.
To document body measurements when a patient is in a wheelchair
Body measurements must be measured accurately, not estimated.
To provide time frames for procedures
Estimating time frames for procedures is not the math skill the textbook describes.

alt.q: A nurse estimates 52 × 19 at about 1,000, but the calculator shows 98.8. What is the best action?
alt.a: Recheck the calculation for an error
alt.ex: The estimate shows the calculator result 'just doesn't look right' (it is off by about tenfold), which is the signal to double-check.
w: Record 98.8, since calculators are exact
Inputs can be wrong. The answer is unreasonable.
Record 1,000, since it is simpler
An estimate is used to check, never to record.
Average the two answers together
Averaging is not a valid check.

alt.q: When estimating 47 × 83, which guideline does the text say to apply first?
alt.a: Round to numbers easy to compute mentally
alt.ex: The first guideline is to round (50 × 80) so the numbers are easy to multiply in your head.
w: Place the decimal point before multiplying
Placing decimals is the fourth guideline, and these are whole numbers.
Expect the answer to be smaller than both
When you multiply whole numbers, the answer should be larger.
Convert both numbers into equal fractions
Not one of the text's guidelines.

items.q: A fraction should be reduced to its lowest terms when
items.a: the numerator and denominator can each be divided by the same number.
items.ex: A fraction can be reduced whenever one number divides evenly into both the numerator and the denominator, as with 2/4 = 1/2. Watch out: 'Dividing by another fraction' is tempting because Table 6–4 ends division with 'reduce if necessary', but the trigger for reducing is a common divisor, not the operation.
w: you want to convert it to a decimal.
Converting to a decimal means dividing the numerator by the denominator. Reducing is not required first.
the numerator is larger than the denominator.
That makes an improper fraction, which is changed to a whole or mixed number. Lowest terms depends on a shared divisor, not on which number is larger.
you are going to divide it by another fraction.
Dividing fractions means inverting and multiplying. Reducing happens at the end, only if necessary.

alt.q: Which fraction is already in lowest terms?
alt.ex: No whole number other than 1 divides evenly into both 7 and 12.
w: Both are divisible by 3, giving 2/3.
Both are divisible by 4, giving 2/3.
Both are divisible by 5, giving 2/3.

alt.q: A student multiplies 2/3 × 3/4 and gets 6/12. What should they do next?
alt.a: Reduce it to lowest terms, 1/2
alt.ex: 6 divides evenly into both 6 and 12, so the answer should be reduced to 1/2.
w: Leave it as 6/12, since it is correct
It is equal in value, but it is not in lowest terms.
Invert it to get 12/6
Inverting is a step in dividing fractions, not multiplying.
Write it as the mixed number 1 1/2
6/12 is a proper fraction less than 1.

items.q: A(n) ______ can be a measurement of weight or volume.
items.ex: In the household system, the ounce measures both volume (an 8-ounce glass of water) and weight (a 6-pound 12-ounce infant). Watch out: Cup is a familiar kitchen measure, but it measures volume only. Only the ounce is used for both.
w: cup
A cup measures volume only.
pound
A pound measures weight only.
yard
A yard measures length.

alt.q: Which example uses the ounce as a measure of weight rather than volume?
alt.a: A newborn weighing 6 pounds 12 ounces
alt.ex: Weight is found by weighing on a scale, as with a 6-pound 12-ounce infant. Liquids are measured by volume.
w: An 8-ounce glass of water at a patient's bedside
Liquids in a glass are measured by volume.
A 4-ounce cup of juice on the meal tray
This is a volume of liquid.
A 1-fluid-ounce dose of cough syrup
A fluid ounce is a measure of volume.

alt.q: Using the equivalent 2 T = 1 oz, how many ounces are in 3 tablespoons?
alt.a: 1.5 oz
alt.ex: Set up the proportion 2 T/3 T = 1 oz/x oz, so 2x = 3 and x = 1.5 oz.
w: 6 oz
This multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
This sets up the ratio upside down (2 ÷ 3).
3 oz
This assumes 1 T equals 1 oz.

items.q: If a physician orders that a patient be given 45 grams of medication, and it is only available in 15-gram tablets, how many tablets should the patient be given?
items.ex: Divide the ordered amount by the strength of each tablet: 45 g ÷ 15 g = 3 tablets. Watch out: This is a simple division. The distractors are close values that catch careless rounding.
w: 2.5 tablets would give only 37.5 g.
3.5 tablets would give 52.5 g, which is too much.
4 tablets would give 60 g, which is too much.

alt.q: A provider orders 0.5 g of a drug. Tablets are 250 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
alt.a: 2 tablets
alt.ex: Convert first: 0.5 g = 500 mg. Then 500 mg ÷ 250 mg = 2 tablets.
w: 0.5 tablet
This divides 250 by 500, which is upside down.
5 tablets
5 tablets would give 1,250 mg, far more than the 500 mg (0.5 g) ordered.
20 tablets
This treats 0.5 g as 5,000 mg.

alt.q: A patient needs 37.5 mg. Scored tablets contain 25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
alt.a: 1.5 tablets
alt.ex: 37.5 mg ÷ 25 mg = 1.5 tablets. A scored tablet can be split.
w: 1 tablet
This gives only 25 mg, too little.
2 tablets
This gives 50 mg, too much.
0.67 tablet
This divides 25 by 37.5, which is upside down.

items.q: Homeostasis means that the body is
items.a: continuously adjusting to changes to maintain balance.
items.ex: Homeostasis is the body's constant adjusting to keep a state of balance. Wellness is experienced when homeostasis is maintained. Watch out: 'Free of disease or disorders' is tempting because homeostasis is linked to wellness, but the term means balance, not being free of disease.
w: in the anatomical position.
Anatomical position is a standard reference posture.
free of disease or disorders.
Being free of disease relates to wellness, which depends on homeostasis, but it is not what homeostasis means.
made up of many complex parts.
Being made of many complex parts describes the levels of organization.

alt.q: On a hot day, a person perspires to keep their internal temperature steady. This best illustrates
alt.a: homeostasis
alt.ex: Perspiring to keep a steady internal temperature is the textbook's example of homeostasis, the body adjusting to keep balance.
w: metabolism
Metabolism is all the chemical processes in the body.
pathophysiology
Pathophysiology is the study of disease.
inflammation
Inflammation is a response to injury or infection.

alt.q: According to the textbook, a state of illness occurs when
alt.a: a control system can no longer maintain balance
alt.ex: Illness occurs when one or more of the body's control systems loses the ability to maintain homeostasis.
w: the body is no longer in the anatomical position
Anatomical position is only a reference posture.
any microorganism is present on the body
Normal flora are always present on healthy people.
body systems begin to work independently
Body systems are always interrelated.

items.q: Two or more organs make up a(n)
items.ex: Two or more organs working together to perform a major function form a body system, such as the urinary or respiratory system. Watch out: Organism is the near miss: it is the next level up, made of systems rather than of organs.
w: tissue.
A tissue is a group of cells with similar functions.
organism.
An organism is the whole being, made of all the body systems working together.
interdependent function.
'Interdependent function' is not a level of organization.

alt.q: Which list shows the levels of organization from simplest to most complex?
alt.a: Cells, tissues, organs, systems, organism
alt.ex: The text builds from cells to tissues to organs to body systems to the whole organism.
w: Tissues, cells, organs, systems, organism
Cells come before tissues.
Cells, organs, tissues, systems, organism
Tissues come before organs.
Organism, systems, organs, tissues, cells
This is the order from most complex to simplest.

alt.q: The stomach wall contains epithelial, connective, nervous and muscle tissue working together. The stomach is therefore best classified as
alt.a: an organ
alt.ex: Two or more types of tissue combined to work together form an organ.
w: a tissue
Several tissue types together make an organ, not a tissue.
a body system
A system needs two or more organs.
an organism
An organism is the whole living being.

items.q: When a patient loses sensation in their toes, which type of cells have been damaged?
items.ex: Nerve cells carry the signals for sensation, and the textbook says loss of sensation indicates damage to the nerves. Watch out: The skin is where touch is felt, so 'Skin' is tempting, but sensation is carried by nerve cells.
w: Blood
Blood cells carry oxygen, fight infection and help clotting. They do not carry sensation.
Bone
Bone cells provide support.
Skin
Skin cells protect the body. Sensation in the toes travels through nerve cells.

alt.q: After a deep cut on the forearm, a patient can feel their fingers but cannot bend them. According to the text, this suggests damage to
alt.a: tendons or muscles
alt.ex: Ch 20: loss of function past (distal to) a wound means damage to tendons or muscles, while loss of sensation means nerve damage.
w: the sensory nerves
Sensation is intact, so the nerves are likely not the problem.
the bone itself
A loss of function sign points to tendons or muscles.
the skin only
Loss of function means damage deeper than the skin.

alt.q: Which cell type is correctly matched with its specialized function?
alt.a: Muscle cells: movement
alt.ex: Ch 7 lists support (bone cells), communication (nerve cells), oxygen transport (red blood cells), movement (muscle cells) and protection (skin cells).
w: Nerve cells: support
Support is the job of bone cells.
Red blood cells: protection
Red blood cells transport oxygen. Skin cells protect.
Bone cells: communication
Communication is the job of nerve cells.

items.q: The fingers are ____ to the wrist.
items.ex: Distal means farther from the reference point (where the limb attaches), so the fingers are distal to the wrist. Watch out: 'Peripheral' suggests 'outer' and is tempting, but the term for farther from the reference point on a limb is distal.
w: deep
Deep means farther from the body surface.
superficial
Superficial means near the body surface.
peripheral
Peripheral means away from the center (for example, edema in the extremities). It does not compare a point on a limb to its attachment.

alt.q: Which statement uses a directional term correctly?
alt.a: The knee is proximal to the ankle
alt.ex: Proximal means closer to the reference point. The knee is closer to the trunk than the ankle.
w: The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The wrist is distal to the elbow.
The ankle is proximal to the knee
The ankle is distal to the knee.
The elbow is distal to the wrist
The elbow is proximal to the wrist.

alt.q: A splint has been applied to a patient's lower leg. According to the text, where should a pulse always be checked?
alt.a: Distal to the splint
alt.ex: Ch 20 says to always check for a pulse distal to the splint, which shows whether blood is flowing past it.
w: Proximal to the splint
This would not show circulation beyond the splint.
Directly under the splint
You cannot reach it, and it would not show flow past the splint.
At the carotid artery only
This does not show circulation in the limb.

items.q: The liver would best be described as
items.ex: The liver is one of the textbook's examples of an organ, which is two or more types of tissue working together. Watch out: 'A group of tissues' is how organs are built, but the question asks what best describes the liver, and the textbook names it as an organ.
w: a group of cells.
A group of cells is a tissue.
a group of tissues.
Organs are built from tissues, but the name of this level, and the textbook's label for the liver, is 'organ'.
a body system.
A body system is two or more organs (the liver is one organ of the digestive system).

alt.q: Which is an example of a tissue rather than an organ?
alt.a: Cardiac muscle
alt.ex: Cardiac muscle is one tissue type. The heart, lung and kidney are organs made of several tissue types.
w: The heart
The heart is an organ.
The left lung
A lung is an organ.
The right kidney
A kidney is an organ.

alt.q: A tissue is best described as
alt.a: similar cells grouped to do a function
alt.ex: Tissues are cells with similar functions grouped together. Tissues then combine to form organs.
w: two or more organs with a major function
That is a body system.
the smallest unit that carries on life
That is a cell.
two or more tissue types working together
That is an organ.

items.q: What is the purpose of the mitochondria?
items.a: To produce energy for cellular processes
items.ex: The mitochondrion, the cell's 'powerhouse', produces the energy used for cellular processes. Watch out: Every option is a real organelle function from the same list. Only 'energy' belongs to the mitochondrion.
w: To assist with the digestion of molecules
Digesting (breaking down) molecules is the job of lysosomes.
To promote cellular reproduction
Cell reproduction is controlled by the nucleus, with centrioles helping in cell division.
To produce protein for cell structures
Proteins for cell structures are made by ribosomes.

alt.q: Which organelle contains enzymes that break down molecules?
alt.a: Lysosome
alt.ex: Lysosomes contain enzymes that help digest (break down) molecules.
w: Mitochondrion
Mitochondria produce energy.
Ribosome
Ribosomes produce protein.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi produces, stores and packages products.

alt.q: A cell that uses large amounts of energy, such as a muscle cell, would be expected to contain many
alt.a: mitochondria
alt.ex: Mitochondria produce the energy used for cellular processes, so high-energy cells need many of them (mainstream knowledge built on the Ch 7 definition).
w: ribosomes
Ribosomes make protein, not energy.
lysosomes
Lysosomes digest molecules.
storage vesicles
Vesicles store and transport materials.

items.q: Physiology is the study of the
items.ex: Physiology is the study of how and why body structures work, which is the function of body systems. Watch out: Anatomy and physiology are always taught together. Anatomy is structure and physiology is function.
w: form and structure of the body.
The form and structure of the body is anatomy.
causes of diseases.
The causes of disease are etiology, and disease processes are pathophysiology.
behaviors that promote health and prevent disease.
Behaviors that promote health describe wellness and health promotion.

alt.q: A student learns how the kidneys filter blood to form urine. This is the study of
alt.a: physiology
alt.ex: How an organ works is function, which is physiology.
w: anatomy
Anatomy covers structure and location.
pathophysiology
Pathophysiology is the study of disease processes.
etiology
Etiology is the cause of a disease.

alt.q: Which statement is an example of anatomy rather than physiology?
alt.a: The femur is the longest bone in the body
alt.ex: Size, shape, names and locations of structures are anatomy. How they work is physiology.
w: The heart pumps blood through the arteries
This describes function.
Red blood cells carry oxygen to the cells
This describes function.
The kidneys filter waste from the blood
This describes function.

items.q: The femur is a major bone in the
items.ex: The femur is the long bone of the upper leg (thigh) and the longest bone in the body. Watch out: Both arms and legs contain long bones. The femur is the leg's, and the humerus is the arm's.
w: hand.
The hand bones are the metacarpals and phalanges (with the carpals in the wrist).
arm.
The arm bones are the humerus, radius and ulna.
foot.
The foot bones are the tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges.

alt.q: Which bone is in the lower leg (calf)?
alt.a: Tibia
alt.ex: The two long bones of the calf are the tibia and fibula.
w: Humerus
The humerus is the upper arm bone.
Femur
The femur is the upper leg (thigh) bone.
Radius
The radius is a forearm bone.

alt.q: Which statement about the femur is accurate?
alt.a: It fits into the acetabulum of the ilium
alt.ex: The text says the femur fits into a cavity of the ilium called the acetabulum.
w: It is the long bone of the upper arm
That is the humerus.
It is a flat bone, like the sternum and ribs
The femur is a long bone.
It is one of the two long bones of the calf
The calf bones are the tibia and fibula.

items.q: Images are projected on which part of the eye?
items.ex: The lens projects the image onto the retina, the innermost layer, which receives it. Watch out: The lens is the near miss: it does the projecting, but the image lands on the retina.
w: Sclera
The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye.
Lens
The lens projects the image, but the image does not land on the lens.
Choroid
The choroid is the middle layer, full of blood vessels that nourish the eye.

alt.q: Which eye structure controls the size of the pupil?
alt.a: Iris
alt.ex: The iris is the colored sphincter muscle that controls the size of the pupil.
w: Cornea
The cornea is the transparent layer that light enters through.
Retina
The retina receives the image.
Sclera
The sclera is the white protective layer.

alt.q: Which list names the three layers of the eye?
alt.a: Sclera, choroid, and retina
alt.ex: The text names the eye's three layers as the sclera, choroid and retina.
w: Cornea, lens, and retina
The cornea and lens are structures, not layers.
Iris, pupil, and lens
These are structures within the choroid.
Sclera, cornea, and the iris
The cornea and iris are parts, not layers.

items.q: What is the major function of red blood cells (RBCs)?
items.ex: Red blood cells carry oxygen, bound to hemoglobin, from the lungs to the body's cells. Watch out: Every option is a real blood or body function. Only oxygen transport belongs to RBCs.
w: Cool the body
Cooling the body is done by perspiration through the skin.
Fight infection
Fighting infection is the job of white blood cells.
Enable blood to clot
Clotting is the job of platelets.

alt.q: Why is enough dietary iron important for red blood cell function?
alt.a: It is needed to make hemoglobin
alt.ex: The text says iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
w: It helps platelets clump to form clots
Clotting is the job of platelets, not iron's role in RBCs.
It lets WBCs engulf bacteria
That is phagocytosis by white blood cells.
It thins the blood so it flows faster
Not stated, and not true.

alt.q: A patient's lab report shows a low platelet count. Which problem is most likely?
alt.a: Bleeding that is slow to stop
alt.ex: Platelets clump to form clots, so too few of them leads to slow or excess bleeding.
w: Poor oxygen delivery to the tissues
This points to RBCs or hemoglobin (anemia).
Frequent infections from bacteria
This points to white blood cells.
A body temperature that stays high
Not related to platelets.

items.q: Secondary prevention focuses on
items.a: treating conditions as soon as they are discovered to prevent further illness.
items.ex: Secondary prevention treats a condition as soon as it is found so that it does not cause further damage, for example antibiotics for an ear infection. Watch out: The rehabilitation option is the near miss: rehab also prevents further disability, but that is tertiary prevention.
w: returning the body to a state of well-being.
Returning to well-being is a general goal, not one of the defined prevention levels.
prevention of the initial onset of disease.
Preventing a disease from starting at all is primary prevention.
rehabilitation to allow patients to regain function and reduce disability.
Rehabilitation to regain function is tertiary prevention.

alt.q: A health fair checks blood pressures and starts treatment for people found to have hypertension. This best illustrates
alt.a: secondary prevention
alt.ex: Finding a condition that already exists and treating it quickly to prevent further damage is secondary prevention.
w: primary prevention
Primary prevention stops the disease from starting.
tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention is rehabilitation after damage.
palliative comfort care
Palliative care relieves symptoms without curing.

alt.q: Which example is primary prevention?
alt.a: Good handwashing to avoid exposure to germs
alt.ex: Primary prevention stops the first onset of disease. The text's example is handwashing.
w: Taking antibiotics to treat an ear infection
This is secondary prevention.
Physical therapy after an accident
This is tertiary prevention.
Cardiac rehab after a heart attack
This is tertiary prevention.

items.q: Which sequence lists the major organs of the urinary system in order as it removes wastes from the body?
items.ex: Urine forms in the kidneys, flows through the ureters to the bladder for storage, and leaves the body through the urethra. Watch out: Ureters and urethra sound alike. The ureters come before the bladder and the urethra comes after it.
w: Urinary bladder, kidneys, urethra, ureters
The kidneys come first, because the bladder only stores urine they have already made.
Urethra, urinary bladder, kidneys, ureters
This starts at the exit (the urethra) and runs backward.
Kidneys, urethra, urinary bladder, ureters
The urethra comes last. The ureters connect the kidneys to the bladder.

alt.q: Which structure carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body?
alt.a: Urethra
alt.ex: The urethra carries urine out of the body. The ureters carry it from the kidneys to the bladder.
w: Ureter
The ureters connect the kidneys to the bladder.
Renal pelvis
This is the collecting part of the kidney.
Nephron
Nephrons filter the blood inside the kidney.

alt.q: A kidney stone blocks the tube between the left kidney and the bladder. Which structure is blocked?
alt.a: Ureter
alt.ex: Each ureter connects one kidney with the bladder, forming a passageway for urine.
w: Urethra
The urethra is below the bladder.
Renal artery
This is a blood vessel, not a urine passage.
Glomerulus
This is a filtering unit inside the kidney.

items.q: Heart attacks are the result of
items.ex: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself, and blockage of these arteries causes heart attacks. Watch out: 'Weakened heart muscles' confuses cause and effect: muscle damage follows a heart attack, but the blocked coronary artery causes it.
w: valves that do not function correctly.
Faulty valves cause murmurs and backflow problems, not heart attacks.
weakened heart muscles.
Weakened heart muscle can result from a heart attack, but it is not the cause.
too much exercise.
Exercise strengthens the heart. It is not the cause of heart attacks.

alt.q: Angina pectoris is heart pain caused by
alt.a: too little oxygen from the coronary arteries
alt.ex: The text defines angina as heart pain from an inadequate supply of oxygen to the heart by the coronary arteries.
w: a heart valve that does not close completely
This describes a valve disorder.
inflammation of the sac around the heart
This describes pericarditis.
a ballooning out of an arterial wall
This describes an aneurysm.

alt.q: Damage to heart muscle from a lack of oxygen is called
alt.a: a myocardial infarction
alt.ex: Ch 20: damage to the heart muscle from a lack of oxygen is called a heart attack, or myocardial infarction.
w: angina pectoris
Angina is the pain from too little oxygen, before tissue dies.
an aneurysm
An aneurysm is a ballooning arterial wall.
a cerebrovascular accident
A CVA is a stroke, which affects the brain.

items.q: Unlike Erikson's stages of growth and development, Piaget's focus was primarily on
items.ex: Piaget's four cognitive stages deal only with children. Erikson's stages cover the whole life span, including adulthood. Watch out: Piaget's last stage runs from 12 years to adulthood, which can tempt 'young adults', but his focus is children.
w: young adults.
Young adults fall under Erikson (intimacy vs. isolation), not Piaget.
middle adults.
Middle adults fall under Erikson (generativity vs. stagnation), not Piaget.
aging adults.
Aging adults are covered by Erikson and Thomas, not Piaget.

alt.q: Which feature does the textbook call unique to Erikson's stages compared with many other theories?
alt.a: They include stages of adult development
alt.ex: The text says Erikson's stages include adult development, which many developmental theories leave out because they focus on children.
w: They focus only on how children think
That describes Piaget.
They assign an exact age to every stage
Erikson did not assign specific ages.
They describe the stages of moral reasoning
That describes Kohlberg.

alt.q: A 5-year-old enjoys pretend play but struggles to see things from another person's point of view. Which Piaget stage fits?
alt.a: Preoperational
alt.ex: The preoperational stage (2 to 7 years) is marked by pretend play and difficulty with logic and other people's views.
w: Sensorimotor
Birth to 2 years: learning through the senses and handling objects.
Concrete operational
7 to 12 years: logical thinking about concrete things.
Formal operational
12 years to adulthood: abstract reasoning.

items.q: Thought, awareness, and the ability to comprehend meaning are referred to as ____ abilities.
items.ex: Cognitive abilities are intellectual processes: thought, awareness and the ability to understand the world and determine meaning. Watch out: Psychological and psychosocial both sound like 'the mind', but thought and comprehension are cognitive.
w: psychological
Psychological refers to emotions, attitudes and other aspects of the mind.
psychosocial
Psychosocial combines psychological (emotional) and social development.
developmental
Developmental is the general term for increasing mental, emotional and social capabilities.

alt.q: A teen starts building close friendships outside the family and joins a team. This mainly reflects which type of development?
alt.a: Psychosocial
alt.ex: Psychosocial development includes social relationships with other members of society and the emotions tied to them.
w: Cognitive
Cognitive development is intellectual processes.
Physical
Physical development is growth of the body.
Motor sensory
Motor sensory development is movement and coordination.

alt.q: Which example best reflects cognitive development?
alt.a: Using problem solving to make a judgment
alt.ex: The text says seeking information and applying it to make judgments and solve problems develops cognitive ability.
w: Feeling anxious before a first job interview
Emotions are psychological.
Growing two inches in height in one year
Body growth is physical.
Joining a club to meet new friends
Relationships are social.

items.q: According to Erikson's stages of psychosocial development, the toddler is in the ______ stage.
items.ex: Toddlers (1 to 3 years) work through autonomy versus shame and doubt. They gain confidence when encouraged to do things like dressing and feeding themselves. Watch out: Initiative vs. guilt is the next stage and is easy to confuse with it. Toddlers are autonomy, and preschoolers are initiative.
w: trust vs. mistrust
Trust vs. mistrust is the infant stage.
initiative vs. guilt
Initiative vs. guilt is the preschooler stage (3 to 6 years).
identity vs. role confusion
Identity vs. role confusion is the adolescent stage.

alt.q: A 2-year-old insists on feeding and dressing themselves. Encouraging this best supports the development of
alt.a: autonomy
alt.ex: Toddlers develop autonomy (confidence in caring for themselves) when they are encouraged to learn independent skills.
w: trust
Trust is the infant's task.
initiative
Initiative is the preschooler's task.
industry
Industry is the school-age child's task.

alt.q: A 4-year-old constantly asks questions and starts new activities. If parents severely restrict this, the child may develop a sense of
alt.a: guilt
alt.ex: The preschooler stage is initiative vs. guilt. Severe restriction can lead to guilt.
w: mistrust
Mistrust belongs to infancy.
shame and doubt
Shame and doubt belong to the toddler stage.
inferiority
Inferiority belongs to the school-age stage.

ord.q: Put Erikson's psychosocial stages in order from earliest to latest.
ord.ex: Erikson emphasized that the stages occur in the same order for each individual. Order: Trust vs. mistrust → Autonomy vs. shame/doubt → Initiative vs. guilt → Industry vs. inferiority → Identity vs. role confusion → Intimacy vs. isolation → Generativity vs. stagnation → Ego integrity vs. despair.

items.q: Which of the following statements is true about Dr. William H. Thomas's work?
items.a: He identifies a cyclic nature to the aging process.
items.ex: Thomas sees aging as a cycle: life begins with 'being', moves through 'doing' and returns to 'being' in elderhood. Watch out: The senescence option uses real Thomas vocabulary ('purest example of being') but attaches it to the wrong group.
w: He breaks the life spans into seven groups.
He uses five groupings, not seven.
Each of his defined life span groups has a specific age range assigned to it.
He deliberately does not assign specific ages to the groups.
He defines senescence as the purest example of being.
The infant, not senescence, is 'the purest example of being'. Senescence is the transition to elderhood.

alt.q: According to Thomas, which grouping's focus is mainly on 'doing'?
alt.a: Adult
alt.ex: Thomas says the adult's focus is on doing, and the most common question between adults is 'What do you do?'
w: Infant
The infant is the purest example of being.
Elderhood
Elderhood returns the person to being.
Senescence
Senescence is the transition out of doing toward elderhood.

alt.q: In Thomas's view, why is elderhood described as a gift of great value?
alt.a: People set aside 'have to do' for 'want to do'
alt.ex: Thomas says elderhood brings a clear preference to set aside the 'have to do' for the 'want to do'.
w: Elders finally gain the most material wealth
Thomas does not say this.
Elders return to the adult focus on doing
Elderhood returns the person to being, not doing.
It is when people first make the move into adulthood
That describes adolescence.

ord.q: Put Thomas's life groupings in order.
ord.ex: Thomas sees aging as a cycle from being, through doing, back to being. Order: Infant → Adolescent → Adult → Senescence → Elderhood.

items.q: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development are based on the theory that
items.a: life consists of conflicts that must be resolved for development to occur.
items.ex: Erikson believed psychosocial development happens by resolving a specific conflict at each stage, which lets the person move on to the next stage. Watch out: 'Same experiences at specific ages' is tempting because the stages occur in the same order for everyone, but not at the same ages or with the same experiences.
w: social development cannot take place without corresponding physical growth.
Erikson's theory is not based on physical growth.
all individuals have the same experiences at specific ages.
Transitions are gradual and individuals differ. Erikson did not assign exact ages.
the behavior expectation of an earlier stage is never repeated.
People under stress may regress to behavior from an earlier stage.

alt.q: A 7-year-old hospitalized with a serious illness starts wetting the bed again. Which statement from the text explains this?
alt.a: Stress can cause regression to an earlier stage
alt.ex: The text says an individual under stress, such as during an illness, may regress to behavior from a previous stage.
w: Each Erikson stage begins and ends at an exact age
Transitions are gradual, not tied to exact ages.
Failing one stage blocks all later growth
A missed stage can still be completed later.
Development stops completely during illness
Not stated. Regression is not a full stop.

alt.q: Which statement about Erikson's stages is accurate?
alt.a: They occur in the same order for every person
alt.ex: Erikson emphasized that the stages occur in the same order for each person, although he did not assign specific ages.
w: They apply only to children under age 12
They include adult development.
A stage not completed can never be completed later
Failing a stage does not prevent completing it later.
They begin and end abruptly at exact ages
The transitions are gradual.

ord.q: Put Erikson's psychosocial stages in order from earliest to latest.
ord.ex: Erikson emphasized that the stages occur in the same order for each individual. Order: Trust vs. mistrust → Autonomy vs. shame/doubt → Initiative vs. guilt → Industry vs. inferiority → Identity vs. role confusion → Intimacy vs. isolation → Generativity vs. stagnation → Ego integrity vs. despair.

items.q: According to Erikson's stages of psychosocial development, an adolescent is in the ______ stage.
items.ex: Erikson's psychosocial stage for adolescence is identity versus role confusion: adolescents are confused about identities as they move from dependent child to independent adult. Watch out: Industry vs. inferiority sits right before adolescence (ages 6-12), so a student who only half-remembers the table picks the neighbor stage.
w: trust vs. mistrust
Trust vs. mistrust is the infant stage (birth to 1 year).
initiative vs. guilt
Initiative vs. guilt is the preschooler stage (3 to 6 years).
industry vs. inferiority
Industry vs. inferiority is the school-age stage (6 to 12 years).

alt.q: A 15-year-old patient keeps changing their style, friend group, and planned career while trying to figure out who they are. According to Erikson, which conflict are they working through?
alt.a: Identity vs. role confusion
alt.ex: Ch 9: adolescents are confused about identities as they move from child (dependent) to adult (independent).
w: Intimacy vs. isolation
Young adulthood (20-40): making commitments to others.
Industry vs. inferiority
School-age (6-12): pride in finished projects.
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt
Toddler (1-3): independent self-care skills.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the task of Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage?
alt.a: Moving from a dependent child to an independent adult
alt.ex: Ch 9 describes adolescence as the transition from child (dependent) to adult (independent) while sorting out identity.
w: Taking pride in finished projects and peer approval
That is industry vs. inferiority (school-age).
Making lasting commitments to a partner and community
That is intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood).
Shifting concern from the self to the next generation
That is generativity vs. stagnation (middle adulthood).

ord.q: Put Erikson's psychosocial stages in order from earliest to latest.
ord.ex: Erikson emphasized that the stages occur in the same order for each individual. Order: Trust vs. mistrust → Autonomy vs. shame/doubt → Initiative vs. guilt → Industry vs. inferiority → Identity vs. role confusion → Intimacy vs. isolation → Generativity vs. stagnation → Ego integrity vs. despair.

items.q: A patient has promised to stop smoking and has joined a gym following a diagnosis of lung cancer. Which stage of grief is the patient experiencing?
items.ex: In bargaining the person bargains for the one thing not possible, more time, and makes promises to be a better person and change bad habits; quitting smoking and joining a gym after a cancer diagnosis are such promises. Watch out: The healthy behavior change looks like positive Acceptance, but promising to change bad habits in exchange for more time is the textbook's Bargaining.
w: Anger
Anger is rage and 'Why me?', often with envy of healthy people.
Acceptance
Acceptance is calm readiness for death, not deal-making to change the outcome.
Denial
Denial is disbelief that the diagnosis is true; this patient is acting on the diagnosis.

alt.q: A patient with terminal heart failure tells the chaplain, 'If I can just live to see my grandchild born, I'll go to church every week.' Which stage of dying is this?
alt.a: Bargaining
alt.ex: Ch 9: bargaining for more time is often done with whomever the person considers the higher being, with promises to live better.
w: Acceptance
Acceptance is peace with dying, not trading promises for time.
Depression
Depression is profound sadness about the losses.
Denial
Denial rejects the diagnosis; this patient acknowledges it.

alt.q: In Kubler-Ross's model, what does the dying person bargain for?
alt.a: More time, the one thing not possible
alt.ex: Ch 9: 'In this stage the person bargains for the one thing not possible - more time.'
w: A cure the providers have not offered yet
The text says time, not a cure.
Relief from pain in the final weeks
Pain relief is not the object of bargaining.
Forgiveness from relatives they hurt
Not the textbook's description of the stage.

ord.q: Put Kübler-Ross's five stages of dying in order.
ord.ex: Not everyone goes through all stages or in this order. Order: Denial → Anger → Bargaining → Depression → Acceptance.

items.q: Entering commands on the computer keyboard instead of using the mouse as a pointer is an effective way to prevent
items.ex: Extensive use of the mouse as a pointing device is a major contributor to RMIs, so the textbook lists learning keyboard commands under ways to prevent repetitive motion injuries. Watch out: Musculoskeletal strain is partly true (RMIs affect muscles and tendons), but the textbook's specific term is repetitive motion injuries.
w: exertion injuries.
Exertion injuries come from lifting, pulling, and pushing, not from pointing devices.
eye strain and visual disturbance.
Eyestrain is prevented by resting the eyes, adjusting contrast, and reducing glare (Box 10-4), not by keyboard commands.
musculoskeletal strain.
Too broad: RMIs do strain muscles and tendons, but the textbook ties keyboard commands specifically to preventing RMIs.

alt.q: A medical coder wants to lower their risk of repetitive motion injury from computer work. Which change matches the textbook's advice?
alt.a: Learn keyboard commands to save and print files
alt.ex: Ch 10 lists keyboard commands (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+P, Ctrl+W) to avoid relying on the mouse.
w: Wear a wrist splint all day even without an order
Splints only when recommended by a physician or therapist.

alt.q: For which person is a BMI reading most likely to be misleading?
alt.a: A very muscular weightlifter
alt.ex: Ch 19: inaccuracy occurs when the individual is very muscular or has lost a lot of muscle mass.
w: A sedentary office worker
No muscle-related inaccuracy.
A healthy 30-year-old
No muscle-related inaccuracy.
An adult of average height and build
No muscle-related inaccuracy.

items.q: Which actions should be taken if you must enter an area in which poisonous fumes are present?
items.a: All these actions should be taken as needed.
items.ex: The textbook lists all three: wear protective breathing gear, use a wet cloth over the nose and mouth if no gear is available, and keep the head above or below a visible cloud of fumes. Watch out: Picking only 'protective breathing gear' misses that the wet cloth and head position are also listed as needed.
w: Cover the nose and mouth with a wet cloth.
Correct but only the backup when no breathing gear is available.
Use protective breathing gear.
Correct but incomplete; the other steps also apply.
Keep the head above or below visible fumes.
Correct but incomplete; the cloud holds the highest concentration of fumes.

alt.q: A rescuer must enter a garage to reach a person overcome by fumes, and no breathing gear is available. What should the rescuer do?
alt.a: Put a wet cloth over the nose and mouth
alt.ex: Ch 20: if no protective breathing gear is available, place a wet cloth over your nose and mouth and take deep breaths of fresh air before entering.
w: Light a match to find the person faster
Fumes may ignite.
Keep their head inside the fume cloud
The cloud holds the most fumes.
Wait until the fumes clear to call help
Delays rescue and EMS.

alt.q: Why should a rescuer keep their head above or below a visible cloud of fumes?
alt.a: The cloud has the highest fume concentration
alt.ex: Ch 20: the cloud will contain the highest concentration of fumes.
w: The cloud is hotter than the room air
Not the textbook reason.
Fumes in a cloud are always flammable
Not the textbook reason.
It keeps the rescuer's eyes from tearing and burning
Not the textbook reason.

items.q: The recommended method to stop bleeding is to apply
items.ex: To stop bleeding, the textbook says to apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile dressing over the area. Watch out: Elevation is also in the procedure, so it tempts; direct pressure is the primary method.
w: elevation of the injured area.
Elevation helps decrease bleeding but is used with direct pressure, not instead of it.
a tourniquet.
Do not use a tourniquet; it can damage tissue and lead to amputation.
several clean cloths.
Adding cloths only helps when they are used to apply direct pressure.

alt.q: Blood soaks through the first dressing on a forearm wound. What should the rescuer do?
alt.a: Add dressings on top and keep the pressure
alt.ex: Ch 20: do not remove the previous dressing; apply more over it and maintain direct pressure.
w: Remove the soaked dressing and replace it with new
Lifting may restart bleeding.
Apply a tourniquet above the wound
Do not use a tourniquet.
Lower the arm below the heart
Elevate above heart level.

alt.q: Bleeding from an arm has not stopped after 15 minutes of direct pressure. What is the next step?
alt.a: Use pressure-point control at the brachial artery
alt.ex: Ch 20: after 15 minutes, use pressure-point bleeding control; for the arm, the brachial artery.
w: Apply a tourniquet a few inches above the wound site
Not used; risks amputation.
Lift the dressing to check the wound
Lifting may restart bleeding.
Apply pressure at the femoral artery in the groin
The femoral pressure point is for a leg wound. For an arm wound, use the brachial artery.

ord.q: Put the steps for controlling external bleeding on a limb in order.
items: Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb
Add dressings on top if blood soaks through
ord.ex: Do not use a tourniquet except as a last resort to save a life. Order: Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb → Add dressings on top if blood soaks through → After 15 minutes, use pressure-point control.

items.q: Which is the best position for an arm or leg that is bleeding heavily?
items.ex: Elevating a bleeding arm or leg above heart level decreases the pressure in its vessels and so decreases bleeding. Watch out: 'Whatever is most comfortable' echoes the discomfort exception, but the default is above heart level.
w: At heart level
At heart level gives no reduction in vascular pressure.
Below heart level
Below heart level increases pressure and bleeding.
Whatever is most comfortable for the victim
Comfort is an exception (discomfort may rule out elevation), not the standard position.

alt.q: Why does the textbook recommend elevating a bleeding leg above heart level?
alt.a: It lowers the pressure in the limb's vessels
alt.ex: Ch 20: elevation decreases the pressure in the vascular system of the arm or leg and so decreases bleeding.
w: It keeps the blood from clotting too fast in the wound
Clotting is wanted.
It replaces the need for direct pressure
Pressure is still applied.
It keeps the person warm and calm
Not the rationale.

alt.q: In which situation should a bleeding leg NOT be elevated?
alt.a: A neck or back injury is suspected
alt.ex: Ch 20: elevate unless contraindicated by neck or back injury, or discomfort.
w: The bleeding is very heavy
Heavy bleeding is when elevation helps.
Direct pressure is already being applied
They are used together.
The person is awake and talking
Not a contraindication.

ord.q: Put the steps for controlling external bleeding on a limb in order.
items: Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb
Add dressings on top if blood soaks through
ord.ex: Do not use a tourniquet except as a last resort to save a life. Order: Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb → Add dressings on top if blood soaks through → After 15 minutes, use pressure-point control.

items.q: Which emergency condition requires the immediate use of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)?
items.a: The injured is not breathing and does not have a pulse.
items.ex: CPR is administered when someone is not breathing and does not have a pulse. Watch out: 'Not breathing but has a pulse' is the near-miss: that is rescue breathing.
w: The injured is not breathing but has a pulse.
Not breathing with a pulse calls for rescue breathing, not CPR.
The injured has suffered a heart attack.
A heart attack victim may still be breathing with a pulse; CPR only if both stop.
The injured is in shock.
Shock is treated with the shock position and EMS, not CPR.

alt.q: An unresponsive person has a pulse but no respirations. Which technique is indicated?
alt.a: Rescue breathing
alt.ex: Ch 20: a person who is not breathing receives rescue breathing; compressions are added only if there is no pulse.
w: CPR with chest compressions
CPR requires no breathing and no pulse.
The Heimlich maneuver
For an obstructed airway.
The shock position
Does not supply oxygen.

alt.q: Once the scene is safe, what is always the first step when approaching an injured person?
alt.a: Check whether they breathe and have a pulse
alt.ex: Ch 20: the first step is always to determine if the individual is breathing and has a pulse.
w: Ask which medications they take
Part of the later history.
Look for a Medic Alert bracelet or necklace first
Done after life threats.
Move them to a comfortable spot
Never move unless necessary.

items.q: Providing emergency care to someone involved in a minor motor vehicle accident is considered __________ and can be performed by individuals who act in good faith.
items.ex: Emergency care given to an accident victim is first aid, and the Good Samaritan Act protects people who give it in good faith. Watch out: 'Good faith' cues the Good Samaritan Act; the care being protected is first aid.
w: cardiopulmonary resuscitation
CPR is only for someone not breathing and without a pulse.
enlisting the help of bystanders
Enlisting bystanders is a helpful action, not the term for the care.
an environmental assessment
Assessing the environment is a step before giving care, not the care itself.

alt.q: What is the goal of first aid, according to the textbook?
alt.a: Minimize the injury's effects until a provider treats
alt.ex: Ch 20: the goal of first aid is to minimize the effects of the injury or illness until the injured can be treated by a provider.
w: Give definitive treatment so that no hospital is needed
First aid is temporary.
Diagnose the injury so EMS can be skipped
Rescuers don't diagnose.
Protect the rescuer from all legal liability
That is the Good Samaritan Act.

alt.q: An off-duty medical assistant presses on a jogger's cut until EMS arrives. The Good Samaritan Act protects them as long as they
alt.a: stay within their ability without gross negligence
alt.ex: Ch 20: protection covers acts within the person's ability, without gross negligence or willful intent to harm.
w: charge only a small fee for the emergency care given
The Arizona example covers care given gratuitously.
hold a license in that same state
It covers any person who helps.
get a signed consent form first
Not a requirement of the law.

items.q: The correct way to remove foreign objects from the eye is by
items.ex: Loose particles are removed by flushing the eye with a large amount of water; cotton swabs and instruments are not used. Watch out: A cotton swab seems gentle, but the textbook forbids it because cotton sheds fibers.
w: grasping them carefully with tweezers.
Do not use instruments such as tweezers; sharp instruments can cause further damage.
rubbing the eye gently.
Do not press on or allow the person to rub the eye.
using a cotton swab.
Do not use cotton swabs; cotton sheds fibers into the eye.

alt.q: A foreign object is embedded in a person's eye and does not flush out. What should the rescuer do?
alt.a: Cover both eyes and await medical help
alt.ex: Ch 20: do not attempt removal; cover both eyes with a dressing, which decreases movement of the injured eye.
w: Remove it gently with clean, blunt tweezers
Removal can create more damage.
Cover only the injured eye snugly
Both eyes are covered.
Have them blink hard and rub it out
Do not rub the eye.

alt.q: Why does the textbook say not to use a cotton swab to remove a particle from the eye?
alt.a: Its fibers can shed and get in the eye
alt.ex: Ch 20: cotton sheds fibers that will get in the eye.
w: Swabs are not sterile enough for eyes
Not the reason given.
Swabs push particles deeper toward the brain
Not the reason given.
Swabs soak up tears that wash particles
Not the reason given.
